papers.title: Confidence-Aware Aggregation for Multimodal Audio Reasoning
papers.abstract: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) enable generative reasoning over complex acoustic scenes but often exhibit prediction instability. We show that this variability can serve as a reliability metric via inference-time self-consistency and confidence-aware aggregation. Using a log-probability--based scoring framework, candidate answers are weighted by model likelihoods, leveraging reasoning diversity and self-certainty without additional training. Experiments on four LALMs, including Qwen3-Omni and Audio Flamingo 3, demonstrate that confidence-aware aggregation improves accuracy and calibration, with additive methods like Borda voting outperforming classical Majority Vote, especially under high disagreement. This approach transforms LALM variability into a source of reliability for scalable and robust multimodal audio understanding. Project code is available at https://github.com/michelolzam/lalm-self-consistency.

papers.title: TTSonic: A Unified Framework for Composable and Controllable Speech Generation
papers.abstract: Modern text-to-speech (TTS) systems can synthesize natural and expressive speech, yet a practical speech foundation model must go beyond naturalness to offer stable quality, precise controllability, and a broad set of composable capabilities within a unified framework. We present TTSonic, a unified speech generation model that supports zero-shot TTS, voice cloning, prosody cloning, instruction following, voice conversion, and cloning from noisy reference speech. Rather than relying on separate task-specific models, TTSonic accommodates diverse conditioning signals, including text, natural language instructions, reference speech, and text-described timbre, within the same model framework. Specifically, we develop a semantic--acoustic disentangled speech tokenizer through ASR-supervised semantic learning and reconstruction-guided generative refinement. Serving as the representational foundation of our unified framework, the tokenizer enables the Text-to-Semantic autoregressive model to focus on semantic and prosodic planning, while the acoustic flow-matching model specializes in high-quality speech rendering under diverse acoustic and timbre conditions. Building on this framework, we incorporate CoT-guided instruction-following planning and Text2Timbre voice design to support controllable speech generation. Experiments across zero-shot synthesis, multilingual and cross-lingual TTS, instruction following, voice design, voice conversion, and noisy-reference cloning demonstrate the competitive performance and broad applicability of TTSonic.

papers.title: VeriSpoof: Beyond Real or Fake with One Audio LLM
papers.abstract: A speech deepfake detector estimates whether a recording is synthetic, but a forensic analyst also asks which system produced it, whether recordings share a source, and what evidence supports each conclusion. We present VeriSpoof, an audio language model that unifies five tasks with shared weights: deepfake detection, generator attribution (generator, acoustic model and vocoder), recording-condition analysis, synthesized-span localisation, and source verification. Each decision is supported by grounded rationales whose statements can be independently verified. Answers are scored by sentence likelihood, allowing detection and source verification to be thresholded without separate heads. Rationale statements can be checked against waveform measurements, span labels, or generator metadata. Counterfactual examples train decisions to follow the stated evidence. Across the 14 Speech-DF-Arena test sets, VeriSpoof-Plus achieves 2.14% pooled EER, ranking third of 28 systems and first among open-weight systems. VeriSpoof-Base, trained only on official training splits of eight corpora, achieves 4.43% EER, less than half that of the next open-weight detector. With the same weights, VeriSpoof-Plus verifies whether recordings from generators unseen in training share a source at 6.2% EER. Controlled studies show that the audio representation governs detection, the LLM governs recording comparison, and source supervision is necessary for neural-codec fakes. Statement-checkable rationales catch partial fakes missed by one-step answers (99.6% vs. 78.4% on PartialEdit) and determine decisions under edits unseen in training (99.5%). Training updates only 29.7M of 2.85B parameters, fitting a single 24 GB GPU with gradient checkpointing. We release both models, inference code, a demo, and VeriSpoof-Bench, the evaluation suite covering these questions.

papers.title: Detector-Guided Vocoder Training for Adversarial Text-to-Speech Synthesis
papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel Text-to-Speech (TTS) framework designed to perform adversarial attacks against speech deepfake detection systems. Given a TTS model and a detector capable of classifying its outputs as synthetic, our approach fine-tunes the vocoder by integrating the detector into the TTS training loop. Unlike traditional adversarial methods that rely on post-hoc perturbations or external noise injection, our approach enables the generation of synthetic speech that is intrinsically adversarial, capable of lowering the target detector's reliability without requiring additional post-processing steps. We evaluate the framework in both white-box and black-box settings, showing its effectiveness against known and unseen detectors. We also propose a multi-detector strategy that allows the system to simultaneously learn to deceive multiple detectors, showcasing the scalability of the method. Experimental results confirm the efficacy of our approach, which has the potential to impact forensic security and detection countermeasures. At the same time, subjective listening tests reveal that the proposed method also enhances synthesized speech quality.

papers.title: Averaging Collusion Breaks Traceability in Personalized Neural Audio Watermarking
papers.abstract: Personalized neural audio watermarking systems embed user-specific payloads into audio to trace the user associated with a leaked or misused copy. Existing evaluations mainly assume access to a single personalized copy, but real-world distribution may expose multiple copies of the same recording. We find that simple sample-wise averaging breaks traceability: averaging only two copies produces tracing-failure rates of 87.7-99.7% across the five systems while largely preserving audio quality. Decoder outputs show distinct responses to coalition payload composition across systems, with high majority agreement in TimbreWM but substantially lower agreement in WMCodec. In a more sophisticated payload-aware setting, mixture weighting can further steer the decoder toward a selected nonmember, achieving a target success rate of 92.3% in TimbreWM. Preliminary confidence screening rejects many collusion-induced assignments while retaining most valid single-copy outputs. Code and results are available at https://github.com/Silwan5z/neural-audio-watermark-collusion-attack. This work highlights multi-copy traceability as an additional evaluation dimension for personalized neural audio watermarking alongside conventional single-copy robustness.
papers.venue: 5 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to ICASSP 2027. Code and results available at https://github.com/Silwan5z/neural-audio-watermark-collusion-attack

papers.title: ReListen: Training-Free Evidence Localization in Hour-Long Audio with Frozen Audio Language Models
papers.abstract: Audio language models are meant to answer questions from the audio itself, but an hour-long recording rarely fits in their context, and the answer often depends on a few seconds of it. Transcribing the recording first makes it fit but discards sounds and voices, while systems that return to the audio must be trained for this behavior. We propose ReListen, a training-free method in which a frozen audio language model finds its own evidence before answering. In a Jev-style scan, the model scores each 20-second window by the probability that it helps answer the question, and it then answers from the highest-scoring minute. This minute overlaps the annotated evidence far more often than transcript retrieval, for 88.5% of VoiceGiraffe questions. Without any change, the same scan also grounds events on LAT-Bench as well as a model trained for temporal grounding. Answering from it matches or exceeds hearing the whole recording with a small fraction of the audio, and on VoiceGiraffe it exceeds a transcript of the whole recording by 9.2 points. The selected evidence is also worth hearing rather than reading. Given the same excerpts, reading their transcript matches listening on speech content, but listening is clearly more accurate on questions about sounds and voices. Moreover, ReListen answers faster than every transcript-based system, and its memory stays constant even for recordings too long to hear whole on one GPU. Therefore, a frozen audio language model can search hour-long recordings by itself, without a transcript or additional training.

papers.title: Technical Evaluations in the Field of AI Music Composition
papers.abstract: AI-based music composition has progressed from symbolic melody generation to systems that produce audio from natural-language prompts, melodic references, or combinations of both. However, the perceived usefulness of a generated track cannot be captured by audio realism alone. A system may sound convincing yet ignore the requested mood, lose musical structure over time, offer little editing control, or provide insufficient information about the provenance of its training data. This paper develops a practical, multidimensional framework for evaluating AI music composition systems. The framework organizes evaluation into five dimensions: audio and musical quality, prompt and structure alignment, controllability and editability, workflow usefulness, and responsible-use transparency. It proposes a staged evaluation protocol combining listening tests, task-based assessment, technical checks, and documentation review. The framework is a conceptual synthesis informed by published work on text-to-music generation, controllable music models, synthetic-music detection, and the supplied systematic review of AI music composition. No new experimental dataset or performance results are claimed. The paper's contribution is an evaluation blueprint that researchers, developers, educators, and music practitioners can adapt before conducting empirical validation

papers.title: PianoBench: Evaluating Musical Perception and Reasoning in Language Models
papers.abstract: Multimodal language models continue to improve on broad music understanding benchmarks, but which musical features can they perceive and reason about? We investigate this question by introducing PianoBench, a benchmark that tasks language models with reasoning about musical performances across congruent acoustic and symbolic input representations. PianoBench is derived from our new multimodal, training-scale dataset comprising more than 20,000 hours of interleaved transcripts of music and spoken musical commentary from instructional piano videos. Open-weight audio-language models achieve at most 52.8% accuracy on PianoBench, and at best only modestly outperform their accuracy on a no-audio control. In contrast, frontier models using chain of thought achieve up to 93.2% accuracy when provided transcripts of music as text, exposing a gap between perceiving musical features from audio and reasoning about musical events when they are given explicitly. We then test whether mid-training on interleaved musical instruction can improve question answering without chain of thought, raising Qwen 3.5 9B Base's zero-shot accuracy on PianoBench with music transcripts from 42.8% to 56.0% after instruction tuning. These experiments suggest that instructional videos may represent an overlooked source of multimodal supervision for music. Available: https://gclef-cmu.org/pianobench.

papers.title: NepTTS-Bench: Native-Speaker Benchmarking and NepaliMOS for Nepali Text-to-Speech
papers.abstract: Nepali TTS has reached a point where multiple systems are available, but there is no shared evaluation to compare them. NepTTS-Bench was created to address what existing automated and manual evaluation systems lack for Nepali TTS. A controlled benchmark with phonological grounding which contains 205 sentences (77 minimal pairs targeting aspiration, retroflex/dental contrasts, nasalization, gemination, and schwa deletion) which is rated by 180 speakers. There are 6,962 ratings for 10 TTS configurations and two human references. Along with this 7 ASR systems were evaluated for round-trip CER. SCOREQ was also run as an automated baseline. The key finding is that automated evaluation like SCOREQ prefers proprietary systems like ElevenLabs but native listeners prefer Piper. This is contributed by the fact that most of the systems not properly tuned for Nepali tend to show Hindi phonological behaviour and our minimal pairs are designed to surface such contrasts. We also present NepaliMOS predictor which is fine tuned on collected ratings. NepaliMOS achieves system-level rho = 0.90 on the dense panel but drops to utterance-level rho = 0.43 under leave-one-system-out evaluation. This is statistically significant and confirms that NepaliMOS captures genuine signal but cross-provider transfer is limited. A human calibration is recommended for new systems for which we release a Python evaluation package for practitioners to run the benchmark against new systems.

papers.title: SciPhi-Chat: Training a Spatial Audio Agent for Question Answering, Dialogue, and Tool Use
papers.abstract: Spatial audio question answering requires associating sound identities with locations and reasoning about their relations. This paper introduces SciPhi-Chat, a spatial audio agent that answers questions, conducts multi-turn dialogue, and calls tools on first-order ambisonic recordings. The accompanying MASU benchmark contains 12,000 samples across 42 task categories, the widest task coverage of any spatial model, with real recordings and simulated audio scenes. SciPhi-Chat achieves a score of 44.9%, 7.4 percentage points above the previous state-of-the-art. On the external ASA-Bench, SciPhi-Chat achieves 74.5% azimuth and 60.0% elevation accuracy, the highest among locally evaluated models. Removing reasoning supervision reduces ASA-Bench accuracy by 17.4 percentage points. All materials will be released via https://github.com/microsoft/sciphi-chat

papers.title: Do Multi-Turn Conversational Capabilities Carry Over from Text to Speech? A Parallel Multilingual Benchmark
papers.abstract: Successful multi-turn voice interaction requires models to retain information from earlier turns, follow persistent instructions, and track revisions to conversational state. These abilities are usually evaluated from transcripts, leaving open whether successes demonstrated from text carry over when the same turns are spoken, and whether this transfer is consistent across languages. We introduce Omnilingua-AudioMC, a strictly parallel multilingual extension of Audio MultiChallenge, to study this question. The benchmark contains 354 conversations and 1,404 rubric items across ten languages, with content, turn structure, cross-turn dependencies, and evaluation criteria aligned across transcript and speech conditions. Across six speech-language models, the shift from reference transcripts to direct speech input is strongly model- and language-dependent: models with similar transcript performance can diverge substantially under speech, and their relative strengths across languages can change. Paired rubric-level analysis shows that aggregate transcript-speech gaps can obscure which conversational requirements are preserved, because losses of transcript-demonstrated successes can be offset by gains on other items. Replacing preceding user turns, the current turn, or both with model-generated transcripts localizes recoverable degradation: for the two models with the largest gaps, history substitution yields a larger macro-level improvement than current-turn substitution in all ten languages, while the strongest direct-speech model gains little from either. These results show that transcript performance is an unreliable proxy for multilingual spoken conversational ability and identify the representation of preceding spoken context as an important source of recoverable degradation. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/QwenLM/Omnilingua-Bench/tree/main/Omnilingua-AudioMC.
reasons: Audio & Speech Language Models: speech-language model

papers.title: ATLAS-Audio Translation for Live Attraction System
papers.abstract: Tourists visiting unfamiliar regions often face language barriers that make it difficult to understand local attractions, historical landmarks, and cultural information. To address this challenge, this paper presents ATLAS (Audio Translation for Live Attraction Systems), a web-based application designed to facilitate multilingual communication through speech processing and language translation. The system integrates speech-to-text conversion, automatic language detection, text translation, and text-to-speech synthesis to transform spoken input into translated audio output. Users can provide audio through the application, obtain a textual transcription, translate the content into a selected target language, and listen to the translated speech. The system is developed using Python and Flask, with dedicated modules for audio processing, speech recognition, language detection, translation, and speech synthesis. In addition, ATLAS incorporates tourism-related information to help users explore destinations and access relevant attraction details in text and audio formats. By combining these capabilities in a centralized platform, the proposed system aims to improve the accessibility of tourism information for people who speak different languages. The application demonstrates the potential of integrating speech technologies and artificial intelligence into tourism support systems. Further evaluation is required to measure translation quality, speech-recognition accuracy, and response time across different languages and real-world acoustic conditions.

papers.title: Cross-Codec Robustness in Speech Watermarking
papers.abstract: Generative speech models synthesize audio that is difficult to distinguish from human recordings. Synthetic speech can be watermarked as a proactive disclosure method, but watermarking models remain vulnerable to resynthesis attacks using neural audio codecs. This article investigates speech watermarking robustness across neural codec and digital signal processing attacks, when specific neural codecs are used for channel augmentation during training. We also present a novel zero-bit watermarking system that uses Descript Audio Codec as the generator. Our results demonstrate that the choice of augmentation codec significantly influences robustness generalization. Experiments show that augmentation with low-bitrate, high-quality neural codecs-Mimi and SNAC-results in promising robustness against unseen neural codecs and traditional attacks with limited quality impact.

papers.title: Route Anything: A Study of Model and Policy Routing for General-Purpose AI Systems
papers.abstract: Artificial general intelligence (AGI) requires a method that can understand, generate, reason, and act across diverse domains and modalities. Rather than relying on a single model to master every capability, a promising path toward AGI now is to orchestrate a heterogeneous ecosystem of specialized models, tools, and policies (candidates) into a unified AI system. At the heart of this vision lies a fundamental question: how can an AI system dynamically select and coordinate the most capable candidate for each task while balancing performance and computational cost? In this work, we present Route Anything, a unified framework for studying model and policy routing across general-purpose AI systems. We develop a unified theoretical foundation that characterizes optimal routing under quality--cost trade-offs and establishes how the information available to a router determines its attainable performance. To systematically investigate routing across diverse capabilities, we first construct an omni-modal trajectory matrix spanning 25 benchmarks across language understanding, image, video, and speech generation, coding and workplace agents, and robotic manipulation, comprising 374,401 scored runs from 452 candidate configurations. Building on this framework, we train and test different routers to investigate the potential of omni-modal model routing, the capabilities of learned routers, and the conditions under which routing improves efficiency. Our results reveal substantial opportunities for capability orchestration: per-input oracle routing outperforms the best fixed candidate by 5.4 points, and learned routers outperform it by 0.3 points across 16 benchmarks, by 2.1 points on video generation, and by 1.1 points on robot manipulation while using 24% less policy time. More importantly, routing raises efficiency by 8.82x on average compared with the reference model.

papers.title: Hybrid acoustic and pretrained embedding feature fusion for unmanned aerial vehicle detection using stacking ensemble learning under a leakage-aware evaluation protocol
papers.abstract: Small multirotor drones produce a characteristic acoustic signature, and microphones offer a low-cost way to detect them. High accuracies have been reported on public drone audio benchmarks, often with random clip-level splits of datasets built from a few long recordings and pieces of existing sound collections, so pieces of one source can appear in both training and test data. We study the binary task of the public DroneAudioDataset (11,704 one-second clips). Its 1,332 drone clips come from 257 five-second chunks of 7 recordings, and 96.4% of its non-drone clips are pieces of the 2,000 clips of the ESC-50 sound dataset. A grouped, source-disjoint protocol (five folds, three repeats) is compared with a random split. Each clip is described by 57 hand-crafted acoustic descriptors, reduced by a hybrid minimum-redundancy maximum-relevance and ReliefF selection or by NSGA-II multi-objective search, and by a 1024-dimensional embedding from the pretrained YAMNet network. Random Forest and XGBoost learners on both views form a stacking ensemble. Under the grouped protocol, the two-view stack reached a mean accuracy of 95.29% (SD 1.62 points over 15 test folds), a specificity of 98.29% and an area under the ROC curve of 0.990, and it correctly classified 98.78% of unseen ESC-50 source clips as non-drone. The random split overstated accuracy by 1.89 to 3.22 points for the four models. Adding YAMNet embeddings to the hand-crafted view raised accuracy by 1.11 points (higher in 12 of 15 folds). Hybrid selection matched the accuracy of all 44 baseline descriptors with 16 to 18 features, and NSGA-II retained 4 to 6 features at lower accuracy. The stack took 51.0 ms per clip on one CPU thread. Source-disjoint evaluation is needed for a fair benchmark on this dataset, and fusing hand-crafted descriptors with pretrained embeddings gives a small but consistent gain at modest computational cost.

papers.title: AI for eGovernance: Leveraging Language Technologies For Digital Inclusion
papers.abstract: The Kenyan government has invested heavily in the digitisation of public service delivery, in line with the Kenya Digital Master Plan 2022-2032. The national eGovernment platform, eCitizen, hosts services that are vital to citizens'livelihoods, including business registration, youth enterprise lending, digital literacy and tax filing. However, the platform faces digital inclusion challenges that limit equitable access for marginalised groups, particularly youth in rural areas and persons with disabilities. This exclusion is driven by a language barrier, since the platform is primarily in English with limited Swahili support, and by a text-only interface that excludes low-literacy and visually impaired users. This paper reports findings from six one-on-one interviews and an eleven-person roundtable discussion across four platforms essential to youth livelihoods: Ajira Digital, Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA) iTax, Higher Education Loans Board (HELB) and the Youth Enterprise Development Fund (YEDF). Drawing on these findings, on Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1 principles as a design lens for diagnosing eCitizen's accessibility gaps, and on comparator models such as Estonia's B\"urokratt and India's Bhashini, the paper proposes a human-centred, systems-minded framework for embedding generative AI and language technologies into eCitizen, including text simplification, neural machine translation, text-to-speech and speech-to-text. The paper argues that, when deployed responsibly with appropriate human oversight, these interventions could meaningfully improve access to government services for linguistically excluded citizens. It also emphasises that AI alone cannot overcome the broader structural barriers, including unemployment and educational inequality, that shape digital exclusion.
papers.venue: 11 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables. Presented at AAIAC 2026, Dar es Salaam, Tanzania

papers.title: Transformer-Based Automatic Speech Recognition Development for Transcription and Clinical Information Extraction in Indonesian on Electronic Health Records
papers.abstract: Integrating Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) into Electronic Health Records (EHR) has the potential to boost the efficiency of clinical documentation by automating the transcription of doctor-patient conversations. However, high-quality transcription doesn't necessarily mean the clinical information will be classified accurately. This study aims to analyze the quality of ASR transcriptions and compare the performance of Machine Learning algorithms in classifying clinical units based on Indonesian clinical texts. The dataset used consists of 1,000 medical records distributed across five clinical units: Cardiology, ENT, General, Internal Medicine, and Pediatrics. Transcription quality was evaluated using Word Error Rate (WER), while classification was done through Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) feature extraction and four algorithms: Random Forest, Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, and Naive Bayes. Model evaluation was carried out using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score on 200 test data. The research results show that the average WER is 0.40%, indicating very good ASR transcription quality. Random Forest achieved the highest accuracy at 44.50%, Logistic Regression 42.00%, Decision Tree 38.00%, and Naive Bayes 32.00%. Random Forest performed best in the Internal Medicine Clinic with a precision of 0.58 and an F1-score of 0.53. These findings suggest that the main challenge lies in the representation of textual features, mainly due to the similarity of medical vocabulary across clinical units. This study highlights the need to develop approaches based on context, clinical entities, ICD-10 codes, and Transformers to improve classification accuracy and support the automation of clinical information management in EHRs. This approach is expected to strengthen semantic understanding, reduce classification errors, and improve system reliability as a supporter of digital clinical documentation in healthcare settings

papers.title: Fuse To Align: Multimodal Representation Learning for Retrieval via Hypergraph Regularization
papers.abstract: Multimodal retrieval must integrate complementary evidence from views that may be missing, noisy, or unequally informative. When a sample provides limited reliable evidence, learning from its views alone can hinder the acquisition of useful retrieval representations. Semantically related training samples may provide complementary observations, yet existing volume-based objectives jointly align modalities within each sample without explicitly enabling information exchange across samples. We therefore propose a training-time hypergraph fusion framework that connects observed modalities both within samples and across semantically related samples, allowing representation learning to draw on evidence beyond an individual sample while leaving the retrieval pipeline unchanged at inference. The framework includes HyVol as a special case and introduces two configurations: wHyVol learns view contribution weights and symmetric semantic affinities, whereas wRHG additionally models typed interactions and participant roles through relational propagation. Missing modalities are omitted rather than imputed, and the hypergraph is discarded after training, incurring no additional inference cost. Experiments on eleven zero-shot video-text and audio-text retrieval benchmarks demonstrate broad improvements with both GRAM and HyperGRAM. Across 17 video benchmark-modality settings evaluated in both retrieval directions, wRHG outperforms GRAM in all 34 comparisons and HyperGRAM in 33 of 34. Mean text-to-video R@1 increases from 63.4 to 68.2 with GRAM and from 64.8 to 68.4 with HyperGRAM, while the largest video-to-text gain reaches 13.3 percentage points on ActivityNet. Under missing-modality evaluation, both weighted configurations retain positive text-to-video gains over GRAM across seven benchmarks at every evaluated missingness rate, even when 90% of clips lack one modality.

papers.title: CrowdForge: Effects of Audio and Visual Audience Participation Modalities on Agency, Collaboration, and Engagement in AI-Mediated MR Performances
papers.abstract: Technology-mediated audience participation (TMAP) enables audiences to influence live performances, yet balancing interaction with meaningful agency remains challenging. While AI-generated music and MR enable new forms of audio and visual audience participation, little is known about how these participation modalities influence audience experiences during live musical performance. In particular, it remains unclear how they shape perceived agency, collaboration, and engagement, and how they complement one another within TMAP systems. We present CrowdForge, an AI- and MR-mediated paradigm where audiences collectively control generative music and virtual environments during a live performance featuring a guitarist and DJ. Through a mixedmethods concert study evaluating three interaction conditions (audio, visual, and combined audio-visual), we demonstrate that observability is the primary driver of audience agency. While visual interaction provided easily observable feedback, audio parameters offered macro-structural control over the music. Audiences tended to use the control enabled by AI audio generation to test musical boundaries, introducing a productive adversarial tension between the crowd and the musicians. This dynamic pushed creative limits, deepened engagement, and generated moments of musical coherence when performers successfully resolved audience-induced challenges. We argue future TMAP systems should prioritize human-centered, highly observable interactions to build agency, while combining the expressiveness of music with the clarity of visual feedback.

papers.title: Be My Ears: Enabling Semantic Alerting for Earphone Wearers with Pheme
papers.abstract: Active Noise Cancellation (ANC) earphones provide immersive listening experiences but induce auditory isolation to earphone users, leaving them vulnerable to hazards and socially disconnected. We present Pheme, an agentic framework that transforms ANC earphones into context-aware auditory assistants. Informed by two user studies (N = 385 and N = 34) that reveal a high prevalence of missed critical sounds and significant linguistic ambiguity (73.6%) in user requests, Pheme employs a three-stage pipeline: (1) an LLM-based Query Understanding module to resolve intent and map ambiguous commands to acoustic targets; (2) Text-conditioned Audio Separation (via SAM Audio) to isolate target sounds from ambient noise; and (3) LALM-based Verification to validate detections against user intent, reducing false interruptions. We evaluate Pheme against a baseline that directly feeds ambient audio into an audio language model for target event detection, using 1,584 audio samples across seven real-world scenarios. Our results show that Pheme achieves 82.2% detection accuracy for user-specified audio events at + 5 dB SNR setup, outperforming the baseline by 9.5% while reducing the false positive rate by 11.9%. Moreover, Pheme significantly reduces operational overhead, cutting API calls by 48.1% and LALM audio processing workload by 67.3%.

papers.title: Reflex: Fast Robot Policy Serving by Reusing and Correcting Past Actions
papers.abstract: Modern robot policies often perform expensive inference to generate action chunks, making serving a latency bottleneck for real-time control and a throughput bottleneck for multi-robot serving. Building on the success of caching in image, video, and audio generation, recent robot-policy advances have reported promising speedups by reusing intermediate denoising states to avoid redundant computation. Surprisingly, we find that such reuse often offers little advantage over simply running fewer denoising steps from fresh noise, without any cache. Moreover, accelerating denoising leaves the expensive policy backbone intact, which can account for 70% of GPU time. We present Reflex, a serving layer that turns past policy executions into a backbone-free path for future decisions. Rather than reusing intermediate computations, Reflex caches complete action chunks to bypass both the backbone and action head. This introduces two challenges: similar observations can demand different actions, and small action deviations (errors) in reuse can compound into execution stalls. Reflex addresses these through two-level cache correction. At the action level, it learns action-aware similarity from past policy decisions, assembles compatible chunks, and applies lightweight residual correction to limit action mismatch. At the execution level, it captures task progress and adaptively refreshes the original policy to limit accumulated errors and balance inference cost. Without modifying the underlying policy, Reflex improves inference latency by 1.4x to 11x and throughput by 2.0x to 2.2x on representative workloads and real robots, while preserving comparable task success.

Weights for **StaleyNET**, a text-prompted music generator trained from random initialization in Rust on NVIDIA edge GPUs. The Transformer, residual vector quantizer, Griffin-Lim vocoder, and GPU kernels are implemented in the project.

The code, paper, and book live in the companion repository:
<https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet>.

## Release v0.1.2

- GitHub release: <https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet/releases/tag/v0.1.2>
- `staleynet-audio` 0.1.2 on crates.io: <https://crates.io/crates/staleynet-audio>. Its page explains each audio step with intuition and runnable examples.
- Since v0.1.1: the GPU kernels are organised into one module per topic, the AGX Thor builds against cuda-oxide's main branch, and the paper has been revised with hardware, benchmark and tokenizer appendices.
- New in these repositories: the `lyrics-thor`, `lyrics-thor-long` and `pq-large` runs, and the band-group token caches they train on.
- CI: rustfmt, clippy with warnings denied, cargo-deny, the audio coverage gate, and documentation tests for every example on the crate page.

The step values are exactly what each `model.json` records. `best/` is the weight-only checkpoint selected by validation. `latest/` is the resumable checkpoint with AdamW moments. Some early runs stored only `best/`, and `thor-base` and `smoke` record step 0 in their `best/model.json`. Where a `latest/` exists, prefer it for the late training state.

### About `pq-large`

`pq-large` is still training on the Jetson AGX Thor (128 GB). The files here are a snapshot at step 7,000 of 20,000, and they will be replaced as the run advances. Its validation loss (5.135 nats per token at step 7,000) is averaged over 16 codebooks of a different tokenizer, so it cannot be compared directly with the 4-codebook runs above.

The model reads codes from the band-group tokenizer, which splits the 128 mel bands into 4 groups and quantises each group with 4 residual levels. That tokenizer is stored as `checkpoints/pq-large/tokenizer.json`, and the matching caches are `cache-g4l4f1/`, `cache-pq-jamendolyrics/` and `cache-pq-recordings/` in the dataset repository. Pass `--cache data/cache-g4l4f1` when generating with this run.

`evaluations/<run>/` holds the paired lyrics test of each lyrics run: the per-track loss with aligned, removed and mismatched lyrics.

## Training progress

The runs on the Jetson AGX Thor publish their metrics here every two hours
(`deploy/hf/publish.sh` in the code repository): `metrics/<run>.jsonl` holds
every logged event, and `plots/<run>.png` shows, from left to right, the
training and validation loss in nats per code against optimizer step, the
latest validation loss of each codebook (coarse levels are far easier to
predict than fine ones), and the throughput in positions per second.

![pq-large training curves](plots/pq-large.png)

## Layout

```text
checkpoints/<run>/best/      weights only       model.json + tensors.bin
checkpoints/<run>/latest/    weights + AdamW    model.json + tensors.bin
configs/                     canonical training configurations
run-configs/                 per-run config.json where the run saved one
metrics/                     full metrics.jsonl for every run
logs/                        captured training logs and the tokenizer sweeps
evaluations/<run>/           paired lyrics evaluations
```

`tensors.bin` is little-endian `f32` in parameter-visitor order. `latest/` appends the AdamW first moments and then the second moments. `model.json` records the tensor manifest, the step, whether optimizer state is present, and the training configuration.

## Download and use

```bash
hf download arpanpathak/staleynet-checkpoints \
  --repo-type model --local-dir staleynet-checkpoints

# From the code repository, on a Jetson with the cuda-oxide toolchain:
cargo oxide build -- --release
staleynet sing \
  --cache data/cache \
  --run staleynet-checkpoints/checkpoints/thor-base/best \
  --prompt "slow acoustic ballad, warm female voice" \
  --out song.wav
```

For the lyrics model:

```bash
staleynet sing \
  --run staleynet-checkpoints/checkpoints/lyrics-orin/best \
  --prompt "grunge rock, raw male voice" \
  --lyrics-file song.txt \
  --out song.wav
```

Architecture: width 256, 8 heads, 6 layers, feed-forward multiplier 4, context length 768, 4 residual codebooks of 1024 entries, 128 mel bands at 24 kHz. `lyrics-orin` adds a 256-byte lyrics field.

## Training data and licensing

- **Song Describer Dataset** (SDD), Zenodo record [10072001](https://zenodo.org/records/10072001): 706 Jamendo recordings with human captions. Captions are CC BY-SA 4.0. The recordings carry the per-track Creative Commons licenses in `audio_licenses.txt`, including CC BY-NC-ND and CC BY-NC-SA.
- **JamendoLyrics MultiLang**, <https://github.com/f90/jamendolyrics>: code and metadata are MIT. Songs and lyrics carry the per-song CC licenses in `JamendoLyrics.csv`.

Because the training audio includes NonCommercial and NoDerivatives tracks, these checkpoints are research artifacts, not a commercial product. Do not use them commercially where the upstream recording licenses forbid it, and do not use them to impersonate a singer without consent.

The checkpoint files are offered under CC BY-SA 4.0 (`LICENSE-CC-BY-SA-4.0.txt`) to the extent the upstream dataset licenses allow. See `NOTICE` for the full provenance statement and `SHA256SUMS` for integrity.

## Known limitations

- Griffin-Lim produces phasey audio compared with a learned vocoder.
- The models are small edge models, not production music systems.
- The lyric models were trained on a small lyrics subset, so lyric intelligibility is limited.
- The checkpoints are research artifacts and have no warranty.

# Model Overview ### Description NVIDIA Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe is an offline speech and audio model that processes recordings, together with text instructions and optional context, into text responses. NVIDIA developed this [Speech-Augmented Language Model (SALM)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.09424) for multilingual transcription, speech translation, contextual transcription, speaker-attributed transcription, rich transcription, timestamp prediction, language identification, and audio question answering. The training mixture also includes a small amount of text instruction following and PII tagging/redaction tasks. This model is ready for commercial or non-commercial use. ### Model Summary | | | |:---|:---| | **Total Parameters** | 34B (4.3B active), including the audio encoder | | **Architecture** | Mamba-2–Transformer hybrid Mixture of Experts language model with a Parallel Expert Encoder (Transformer ASR encoder and speaker encoder) | | **Precision** | BF16 (full-precision reference weights); [FP8](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B-FP8) and [NVFP4](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B-NVFP4) variants are available | | **Context Length** | 65,536 tokens; recordings up to 1 hour | | **Inputs / Outputs** | Audio and text / text, with optional word timestamps | | **Languages** | 40; see the [language support matrix](#language-support-matrix) | | **Tasks** | Transcription in verbatim or written form, contextual transcription, speaker-attributed transcription, rich transcription, speech translation, language identification, and audio question answering | | **Deployment** | 1× H100 80 GB; see the [hardware compatibility table](#software-integration) | | **Speculative Decoding** | Native Multi-Token Prediction (MTP); optional DFlash2 draft model | | **Reasoning Mode** | Configurable through the chat template (`enable_thinking=True/False`) | | **Recommended Sampling** | Transcription, translation, and language identification: temperature 0, reasoning off; audio understanding: temperature 0.6, top_p 0.95, reasoning on | | **Best For** | Highest accuracy, customization, and fine-tuning | | **License** | [OpenMDW-1.1](https://openmdw.ai/license/1-1/) | ### Results at a Glance Results captured on October 12, 2026. These serving optimizations are not yet part of the open-source release; we aim to upstream them to NeMo Speech and vLLM at a later date. The perception configuration uses a 1,280-dimensional identity connector followed by a learned projection to 2,688 dimensions. Audio features are combined with the text prompt for text generation. The model enables joint multi-token prediction (MTP), with two trained next-token prediction depths using a repeated layer and retaining the existing head. Reusing the repeated layer during inference supports up to eight speculative tokens. Use this software and the retrieved materials at your own risk. ### vLLM Linux inference runtimes, including vLLM and Hugging Face Transformers, can also run on Windows through WSL2. GGML supports both Linux and native Windows. See [hardware, runtime, and operating system compatibility](#software-integration). #### Environment Setup Inference requires **vLLM 0.32.0** and the latest NeMo Speech main branch, which provides the vLLM plugin for this model. Install both into one environment with [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) and download the checkpoint: ```bash git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Speech.git nemo-speech cd nemo-speech uv venv --python 3.13 .venv UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=$PWD/.venv uv sync --extra asr --extra vllm --locked --no-install-project uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python --no-deps -e . # PyAV decodes compressed audio formats, such as M4A, without a system FFmpeg. uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python --no-deps av==19.0.2 # vLLM requires OpenCV, which NeMo's dependency settings exclude. uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python --no-deps opencv-python-headless==5.0.0.93 source .venv/bin/activate hf download nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B --local-dir ./NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B ``` #### Start the Server Start an OpenAI-compatible server on one GPU, with MTP speculative decoding proposing eight tokens (MTP8): ```bash export VLLM_PLUGINS=nemo_speechlm # Allow vLLM to decode recordings up to one hour long (the default is 600 seconds). export VLLM_MAX_AUDIO_DECODE_DURATION_S=3600 export VLLM_MAX_AUDIO_CLIP_FILESIZE_MB=180 # Word timestamps require the V1 model runner. export VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0 vllm serve ./NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B \ --served-model-name nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B \ --trust-remote-code --dtype bfloat16 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.94 \ --max-model-len 65536 --max-num-batched-tokens 4096 --max-num-seqs 192 \ --enable-chunked-prefill --no-enable-prefix-caching \ --use-replayssm --mamba-backend flashinfer --mamba-cache-mode none \ --mm-processor-cache-gb 0 --no-async-scheduling \ --limit-mm-per-prompt '{"audio":{"count":6,"length":120000000}}' \ --speculative-config '{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":8}' \ --reasoning-parser nemotron_v3 \ --trust-request-mm-kwargs \ --middleware nemo.collections.speechlm2.vllm.salm.ctc_serving.ctc_timestamp_middleware ``` The server listens on `127.0.0.1:8000`; use `--host` and `--port` to change this. The settings target an H100 with 80 GB of GPU memory; other hardware or workloads may need a different `--gpu-memory-utilization`, `--max-model-len`, or `--max-num-seqs`. The `--middleware` and `--trust-request-mm-kwargs` options let requests opt into [word timestamps](#word-timestamps-and-speaker-diarization). To change the configuration, modify the command as follows: | Configuration | Change | | --- | --- | | Eight GPUs: one data-parallel engine per GPU, with expert parallelism (TP=1, DP=8, EP=8) | Add `--data-parallel-size 8 --api-server-count 8 --enable-expert-parallel --disable-custom-all-reduce` | | MTP with two proposed tokens (MTP2) | Set `"num_speculative_tokens":2` | | No speculative decoding | Remove `--speculative-config` | #### Speculative Decoding Speculative decoding proposes several tokens at once and verifies them with the main model. The checkpoint contains two MTP depths implemented with a repeated layer. MTP8 reuses that layer to propose eight tokens; it does not require eight distinct trained MTP layers. The best mode depends on the GPU and the workload. Approximate throughput for batched English ASR on **one NVIDIA H100 80 GB**, using tuned serving settings: | Decoding mode | Approximate BF16 RTFx | | --- | ---: | | MTP off | Not measured | | MTP2 | 410 | | MTP8 | 270 | | DFlash2 K=7 | 340 | | DFlash2 K=15 | 260 | RTFx is total audio duration divided by processing time: 340 RTFx means about 340 seconds of audio processed per second under batch load. These are rough throughput estimates, excluding server startup, for the English Open ASR and Monsoon datasets with reasoning disabled. Throughput depends on recording length, output length, batch size, and GPU memory settings; it is not a single-request latency estimate. Keep ReplaySSM (`--use-replayssm --mamba-backend flashinfer --mamba-cache-mode none`) and prefix caching disabled, as in the command above. The first requests after startup are slower while kernels are compiled and warmed up.
DFlash2 draft model As an alternative to MTP, the separate draft model [`nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B-DFlash2`](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B-DFlash2) proposes up to 15 tokens at once with vLLM's `dflash` method. DFlash2 and MTP are alternatives and are not combined. K=7 is the recommended starting point; K=15 was slower on the tested ASR workload. vLLM 0.32.0 needs a small fix to its DFlash2 implementation; without it, the server can fail when requests finish. Apply it once to the environment: ```bash python - <<'EOF_PATCH' from pathlib import Path import vllm path = Path(vllm.__file__).parent / "model_executor/models/qwen3_dflash2.py" source = path.read_text() if "safe_anchor_token_ids" not in source: old = " successors = successor_table[candidate_ids]\n" anchor = " anchor_token_ids[:, None, None].expand(-1, 1, top_k)," assert source.count(old) == 1 and source.count(anchor) == 1, "unexpected vLLM version" source = source.replace(old, ( " safe_anchor_token_ids = anchor_token_ids.clamp(\n" " min=0, max=predecessor_table.shape[0] - 1\n" " )\n" + old )).replace(anchor, " safe_anchor_token_ids[:, None, None].expand(-1, 1, top_k),") path.write_text(source) EOF_PATCH ``` The fix modifies vLLM source code (Copyright contributors to the vLLM project), which is licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0, not under OpenMDW-1.1; see [THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md](THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md). Then start the server with the following options instead of `--speculative-config` and `--middleware` from the command above. Word timestamps are not available with DFlash2, so the CTC alignment is disabled: ```bash --speculative-config '{"method":"dflash","num_speculative_tokens":7,"model":"nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B-DFlash2"}' \ --hf-overrides '{"ctc_timestamps":{"enabled":false}}' ``` vLLM runs DFlash2 only on its V2 model runner, so also run `unset VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER` before starting the server.
#### Send a Request Send audio to the `/v1/chat/completions` endpoint with an OpenAI-compatible client. The following function covers transcription, reasoning, and word timestamps: ```python import base64 from pathlib import Path from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI(base_url="http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1", api_key="EMPTY") def ask(audio_path, prompt, system_prompt="", reasoning=False, timestamps=False): audio = base64.b64encode(Path(audio_path).read_bytes()).decode() messages = [{"role": "system", "content": system_prompt}] if system_prompt else [] messages.append({"role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "text", "text": prompt}, {"type": "audio_url", "audio_url": {"url": f"data:audio/wav;base64,{audio}"}}, ]}) extra_body = { "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": reasoning}, "skip_special_tokens": False, # keep speaker and event tags "spaces_between_special_tokens": False, "seed": 0, } if reasoning: extra_body.update(top_k=-1, thinking_token_budget=17408) extra_body["chat_template_kwargs"]["reasoning_budget"] = 16384 if timestamps: extra_body["mm_processor_kwargs"] = {"capture_ctc_timestamps": True} return client.chat.completions.create( model="nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B", messages=messages, temperature=0.6 if reasoning else 0, top_p=0.95 if reasoning else 1.0, max_tokens=20480 if reasoning else 16384, extra_body=extra_body, ) response = ask("audio.wav", "Transcribe the following audio.") print(response.choices[0].message.content) ``` A dense one-hour conversation can need about 20,000 output tokens. For long recordings, raise `max_tokens` or remove it, so that the transcript is not truncated. Transcription uses temperature 0 with reasoning disabled. For audio understanding, enable reasoning and ask a question about the audio: ```python response = ask("audio.wav", "What is happening in this audio?", reasoning=True) ``` This sets temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, top-k disabled, seed 0, a 20,480-token completion limit, and a 16,384-token reasoning budget with a 1,024-token allowance to finish reasoning. Use the task instructions documented under [Evaluation Prompts](#evaluation-prompts) as `prompt` and `system_prompt`. #### Word Timestamps and Speaker Diarization The checkpoint bundles the CTC heads used to align the generated transcript to the audio. With `--middleware` set as in the server command above, request timestamps with `timestamps=True`, together with a speaker-tagged transcription prompt: ```python response = ask("audio.wav", ( "Transcribe this audio with punctuation and capitalization. " "Include all spoken words and verbal fillers. " "Write numbers in their standard written form. " "Put speaker tags on the transcription." ), timestamps=True) alignment = response.model_dump()["ctc_timestamps"] if alignment["error"] is not None: raise RuntimeError(alignment["error"]) for word in alignment["words"]: print(word["word"], word["start"], word["end"], word["speaker"]) ``` The response contains a top-level `ctc_timestamps` object: - `words`: word text, start and end times in seconds relative to the input audio, and the transcript's speaker tag. - `diarization`: speaker activity segments derived from the audio. - `speaker_tag_to_diarization_speaker`: the mapping between transcript tags and diarization speakers. - `error`: `null` on success, or an alignment failure reason. Check this field before using the timestamps. Timestamp requests accept one audio recording, `stream=false`, and `n=1`. Keep `skip_special_tokens=false` and ask for speaker tags when speaker attribution is needed. A transcript without speaker tags is aligned as a single speaker. Use the `diarization` segments, rather than word timestamps, when evaluating diarization. ### SGLang-Omni [SGLang-Omni](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni) serves this model for whole-file transcription on `/v1/audio/transcriptions`, on one GPU, from the BF16 or FP8 checkpoint (both validated on one H100 80 GB and one RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell). It does not need NeMo. After [installing SGLang-Omni](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni/blob/main/docs/get_started/installation.md) 0.2.0, which pins SGLang 0.5.22: ```bash sgl-omni serve \ --model-path nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B \ --model-name nemotron-transcribe \ --mem-fraction-static 0.85 \ --port 8000 curl http://localhost:8000/v1/audio/transcriptions \ -F model=nemotron-transcribe \ -F file=@audio.wav ``` Word timestamps, speaker-attributed output, translation and speculative decoding are not part of this integration. See the [SGLang-Omni Nemotron Transcribe cookbook](https://sgl-project.github.io/sglang-omni/cookbook/nemotron_transcribe.html) for its settings, streaming and a tuned profile for short clips. ### Transformers usage 🤗 Install 🤗 Transformers from source: ```sh pip install git+https://github.com/huggingface/transformers ```
Transcription ```python from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoProcessor model_id = "nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B" samples = "https://huggingface.co/datasets/hf-internal-testing/dummy-audio-samples/resolve/main/" processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id) model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, device_map="auto") audio = [samples + "en-Alice_woman.wav", samples + "diarization_example.mp3"] speaker_attributed_prompt = ( "Transcribe this audio with punctuation and capitalization. Include all spoken words and verbal fillers. Write " "numbers in their standard written form. Put speaker tags on the transcription." ) prompt = [None, speaker_attributed_prompt] inputs = processor.apply_transcription_request(audio, prompt=prompt).to(model.device) outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=1024) texts = processor.decode(outputs[:, inputs.input_ids.shape[1] :], skip_special_tokens=False) print([text.replace(processor.tokenizer.pad_token, "") for text in texts]) ```
Speaker-attributed transcription ```python from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoProcessor model_id = "nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B" samples = "https://huggingface.co/datasets/hf-internal-testing/dummy-audio-samples/resolve/main/" processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id) model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, device_map="auto") prompt = ( "Transcribe this audio with punctuation and capitalization. Include all spoken words and verbal fillers. Write " "numbers in their standard written form. Put speaker tags on the transcription." ) conversation = [ { "role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "text", "text": prompt}, {"type": "audio", "path": samples + "diarization_example.mp3"}, ], } ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( conversation, tokenize=True, add_generation_prompt=True, return_dict=True, enable_thinking=False, ).to(model.device) outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=1024) text = processor.decode(outputs[0, inputs.input_ids.shape[1] :], skip_special_tokens=False) print(text) ``` `processor.extract_speaker_dict` splits the output into one dictionary per speaker turn: ```python for turn in processor.extract_speaker_dict(text): print(turn) ```
Word timestamps and speaker diarization Requires `torchaudio` and `scipy`. ```python from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoProcessor model_id = "nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B" samples = "https://huggingface.co/datasets/hf-internal-testing/dummy-audio-samples/resolve/main/" processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id) model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, device_map="auto") prompt = ( "Transcribe this audio with punctuation and capitalization. Include all spoken words and verbal fillers. Write " "numbers in their standard written form. Put speaker tags on the transcription." ) inputs = processor.apply_transcription_request(samples + "diarization_example.mp3", prompt=prompt).to(model.device) outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=1024, return_word_timestamp_logits=True) texts = processor.decode(outputs.sequences[:, inputs.input_ids.shape[1] :], skip_special_tokens=False) timestamps = processor.align_word_timestamps( texts, outputs.word_timestamp_logits, inputs.input_features_mask, outputs.speaker_logits, ) print(timestamps[0]["chunks"][:3]) ```
See the [Transformers documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/nemotron3_5_transcribe) for more. ### Evaluation Prompts Use these shortened task-specific templates as starting points. For ASR evaluation, use [Exact ASR Benchmark Prompts](#exact-asr-benchmark-prompts). The ASR benchmark environment uses vLLM 0.28.0 and NeMo Speech with the FP32 preservation change from [PR #16357](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Speech/pull/16357), which is included in the main branch, with MTP2. For audio understanding, spoken instructions, and text reasoning, use [Exact Understanding and Reasoning Prompts](#exact-understanding-and-reasoning-prompts), which lists the complete evaluated system prompts; keep the prepared user questions and choices unchanged. For the remaining benchmark families, use [All Evaluated Prompts](#all-evaluated-prompts), which contains the complete evaluated prompts and reasoning flags. Replace placeholders with the actual languages, labels, or context. #### Prompt Recommendations For these tasks, keep the **system prompt empty**. Send the instruction in the **user message**, alongside the audio. | Task | Recommended user prompt | Why we suggest it | | --- | --- | --- | | Verbatim ASR, including multilingual and long-form audio | `Audio transcription. Language: as spoken. Wording: verbatim, including fillers and repetitions. Formatting: punctuation and capitalization. Output: transcript only.` | Preserves wording and language with an explicit output format. | | Clean written transcript | Replace the wording clause above with `omit fillers and accidental repetitions; keep the remaining spoken wording unchanged`. Add `numbers in their standard written form` if needed. | Makes cleanup and number normalization explicit. | | Speaker attribution / word timestamps | `Transcribe this audio with punctuation and capitalization. Include all spoken words and verbal fillers. Write numbers in their standard written form. Put speaker tags on the transcription.` | Provides stable speaker tags for attribution and timestamp alignment; also enable timestamp capture. | | Near-field speaker only (experimental) | `Transcribe this audio. Do not transcribe any other voices.` | Ignores background voices, such as far-field speech in a meeting room. --- license: apache-2.0 language: - as - bn - en - gu - hi - kn - ml - mr - or - pa - ta - te pipeline_tag: text-to-speech base_model: Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B-Base tags: - text-to-speech - tts - indic - multilingual - voice-cloning - streaming - streaming-tts - multilingual-tts - indian-languages - voice-agents - speech-synthesis - text-normalization - hindi-tts - mimi - maya3 --- # Maya 2 Native: Streaming Text-to-Speech for Indian Languages Maya 2 Native is an **open-weight multilingual text-to-speech (TTS) model for 11 Indian languages and English**. It generates **24 kHz speech**, streams audio as it is produced, and supports **20 built-in voices**, **zero-shot voice cloning** and **cross-lingual speech synthesis**. Model weights and inference code are released under **Apache-2.0**. Assamese is cross-lingual for every built-in voice; see [limitations](#limitations). ## Quickstart Use **Linux, Python 3.10–3.12, and an NVIDIA GPU with a driver supporting CUDA 12.8**. Start with `max_seats=1`. The documented single-seat loading peak is approximately 9.2 GB plus CUDA context; a 12 GB or larger GPU provides more room. See [hardware and memory](#hardware-and-memory) before increasing concurrency. ```bash python -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate pip install "maya3[server] @ git+https://github.com/MayaResearch/maya2-native" \ --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128 ``` ### Generate speech ```python import soundfile as sf from maya3 import Maya3TTS tts = Maya3TTS.from_pretrained("maya-research/maya2-native", max_seats=1) audio = tts.generate( "नमस्ते, आपका ऑर्डर कल पहुँच जाएगा।", lang="hi", voice="Ahana", normalize=True, ) sf.write("speech.wav", audio, 24000) tts.close() ``` `generate()` returns a mono NumPy waveform in `float32`. Model weights, the Mimi codec, and the ECAPA speaker encoder are downloaded on first use. For offline inference, cache all three first, then set `HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1`. **Normalization differs by interface:** the HTTP and WebSocket servers enable it by default. The Python API requires `normalize=True`. It expands numbers, currency, dates, times, URLs, email addresses, and other written forms into spoken text. Check the output for unusual formats.
Stream audio as it is generated ### Stream speech ```python from maya3 import Maya3TTS tts = Maya3TTS.from_pretrained("maya-research/maya2-native", max_seats=1) try: with open("speech.pcm", "wb") as output: for chunk in tts.stream( "Your order has shipped and will arrive tomorrow.", lang="en", voice="Siddhant", normalize=True, ): output.write(chunk.astype(" ### Clone a voice across languages Use a clean, single-speaker reference clip and its exact transcript. Obtain the speaker's permission before cloning their voice. The reference language and the output language can differ. ```python import soundfile as sf from maya3 import Maya3TTS tts = Maya3TTS.from_pretrained("maya-research/maya2-native", max_seats=1) tts.register_voice( "my_voice", ref_audio="reference.wav", # 3–10 seconds recommended ref_text="", lang="hi", # reference language ) audio = tts.generate( "வணக்கம், எப்படி இருக்கிறீர்கள்?", lang="ta", # output language voice="my_voice", normalize=True, ) sf.write("cloned_voice_tamil.wav", audio, 24000) tts.close() ``` The default cloning mode, `icl_spk`, combines the reference audio with an ECAPA speaker embedding. Clones approximate the reference voice; similarity and accent vary. A dedicated cloning benchmark is not included in this release's reported results.
Run a local HTTP and WebSocket server ### Serve over HTTP or WebSocket ```bash python -m maya3.server \ --ckpt maya-research/maya2-native \ --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 --max-seats 1 ``` After `GET /health` reports ready, generate speech: ```bash curl --fail-with-body -sS http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/audio/speech \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"input":"Your order has shipped.","language":"en","voice":"Ahana","response_format":"wav"}' \ --output speech.wav ``` The server provides `POST /v1/audio/speech`, `WS /v1/tts/stream`, and voice registration endpoints. It has no built-in authentication; add authentication and access controls before exposing it beyond a trusted environment. See the [GitHub README](https://github.com/MayaResearch/maya2-native#serve-the-model) for clients and protocol details.

Three ASR judges measured intelligibility; a speaker-embedding classifier measured consistency among the 20 built-in voices. **These are Maya Research's release measurements.** ASR error rates and embedding similarity capture specific aspects of quality; they do not replace human listening or measure every aspect of naturalness. Serving measurements below describe the tested hardware and workload. ### Benchmark design The release benchmark, **bench6k**, contains **6,000 held-out texts: 500 per language across 31 content categories**, including conversation, names, numbers, dates, currency, addresses, URLs, code-mixed text, tongue twisters, and prompts of 1–50 words. The release documentation states that these evaluation texts were excluded from training. The benchmark produced **20.3 hours of speech** through the server, with normalization and engine guards enabled, sampled decoding, and one seed per row. Voices were distributed across languages and categories; long inputs used the serving stack's text chunking. Three ASR systems transcribed the generated speech: - **ASR-1:** Maya's in-house Indic ASR and primary judge. - **Qwen3-ASR:** a third ASR judge. - **ASR-2:** a second in-house Indic ASR, held out from training, reward generation, and checkpoint selection. **Character error rate (CER)** compares ASR transcripts with spoken-form references. Scorer v1 uses the benchmark's normalization and script harmonization. Scorer v2 additionally harmonizes Latin and native-script spellings in code-mixed spans. Architecture and audio generation ## Architecture Maya 2 Native generates discrete audio tokens autoregressively, then decodes them into speech with Mimi. | Component | Description | |---|---| | Text and audio backbone | Initialized from [Qwen3-1.7B-Base](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B-Base); 28 layers, hidden size 2,048, 16 attention heads and 8 KV heads; extended vocabulary for language and audio tokens | | Depth decoder | Approximately 555M parameters; predicts codebooks 1–31 after the backbone predicts codebook 0 | | Audio codec | [Kyutai Mimi](https://huggingface.co/kyutai/mimi); 32 codebooks with 2,048 entries each, at 12.5 frames per second | | Speaker conditioning | 192-dimensional [SpeechBrain ECAPA-TDNN](https://huggingface.co/speechbrain/spkrec-ecapa-voxceleb) embedding projected into the backbone; reference-audio conditioning for cloning | | Output | 24 kHz mono speech, 80 ms per audio frame | At each step, the backbone predicts the first codebook, the depth decoder fills the remaining codebooks, and Mimi decodes an audio frame. The engine can emit that frame while generation continues. An end-of-audio token controls normal stopping; duration and loop guards provide additional controls.
## Training data and procedure The release documentation describes a mixture of **licensed and synthetic speech with transcripts** across the 12 languages, plus text-only data used to adapt the backbone to the languages. The built-in voice personas use synthetic and licensed voice data prepared for this purpose. The preference-optimization stage used **direct preference optimization (DPO)** on model-generated candidates ranked by ASR agreement and speaker similarity. Benchmark texts were excluded from training, according to the release documentation. Dataset identities, total training hours, detailed per-language composition, and the full training configuration are not disclosed in this release. Automated scores should be considered alongside these disclosure limits. ## Limitations - **Uneven language coverage.** Assamese is the most challenging Indic language in the release benchmark. No built-in voice has at least one hour of Assamese training data; some outputs drift toward a Bengali-like timbre. Other cross-lingual combinations can also carry the voice's training-language accent. - **Very short turns.** One- or two-word prompts are less stable in voice identity, and speaker-embedding evaluation is less reliable on very short clips. A slightly longer phrase may help short agent responses. - **Code-mixed and written-form inputs.** English words inside Indic sentences vary by voice. URLs, symbols, dates, and long digit sequences remain difficult, even with normalization. Listen to application-specific examples before relying on them. - **Voice cloning.** Similarity is approximate. Noise, multiple speakers, short references, and inaccurate transcripts can degrade results. Dedicated zero-shot cloning scores are not reported here. - **Emotion and events.** Tags such as `[laughs]`, `[sighs]`, `[whispers]`, `[sad]`, and `[excited]` are best effort and were not the focus of this release. - **Generation and guards.** Sampling can produce errors. The same seed is reproducible for an isolated request, but batching changes the random stream. Loop and duration guards can end genuinely repetitive text early. No benchmark clip spoke a built-in voice name aloud, but this remains a possible failure mode. - **Evaluation scope.** Results use automated ASR and speaker-embedding judges. This card does not report a human naturalness study, comprehensive dialect or demographic evaluation, confidence intervals, or a controlled comparison with other TTS models. ## Intended use and responsible deployment Maya 2 Native is intended for voice interfaces and agents, accessibility, reading and narration, IVR, notifications, and research on multilingual speech generation. Clone only voices you own or have explicit permission to use. Disclose synthetic speech to listeners, especially in calls and media. Do not use the model for deceptive impersonation, fraud, harassment, non-consensual content, disinformation, or attempts to defeat voice authentication. Confucius4-TTS: a Multilingual and Cross-Lingual Zero-Shot TTS Engine

One voice. Any language.

                                  

Confucius4-TTS is an advanced LLM-based text-to-speech (TTS) system designed for multilingual and cross-lingual speech synthesis. Built on a speech encoder + large language model (LLM) architecture, Confucius4-TTS enables high-quality speech generation while preserving speaker identity across languages. You can try our online demo at **[https://huggingface.co/spaces/CharlesW/Confucius4-TTS](https://huggingface.co/spaces/CharlesW/Confucius4-TTS)**. **✨ Key Features** - **14 Languages Supported**: Chinese, English, Japanese, Korean, German, French, Spanish, Indonesian, Italian, Thai, Portuguese, Russian, Malay and Vietnamese *(more coming soon)* - **Unconstrained Voice Cloning**: No reference transcript required - **Cross-Lingual Voice Transfer**: Unaccented speech synthesis across 14 languages - **Zero-Shot Voice Transfer**: Clone voices without additional training - **Seamless Emotion Transfer**: Clone the feeling, not just the voice - **Robust Generalization**: Stable performance in real-world multilingual scenarios With strong cross-lingual generalization, Confucius4-TTS allows users to seamlessly switch languages while keeping the same voice, delivering fluent, natural, and expressive speech. ## Contents - [Installation](#-installation) - [Inference](#-inference) - [Training](#-training) - [Performance](#-performance) - [Citation](#citation) ## 🛠 Installation ### Requirements - Python 3.10 - CUDA 12.6 ### Setup 1. Clone the repository: ```bash git clone https://github.com/netease-youdao/Confucius4-TTS.git cd Confucius4-TTS ``` 2. Create and activate a conda environment: ```bash conda create -n confuciustts python=3.10 -y conda activate confuciustts ``` 3. Install dependencies: ```bash pip install -r requirements.txt ``` ## 🚀 Inference Use the provided `example.py` script for zero-shot TTS synthesis: ```bash python example.py \ --prompt_wav path/to/reference.wav \ --text "Your text to synthesize" \ --lang en \ --out output.wav \ --config config/inference_config.yaml ``` You can also use the Python API directly: ```python import torch import torchaudio from confuciustts.cli.inference import ConfuciusTTS model = ConfuciusTTS( config_path="config/inference_config.yaml", device="cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu", ) audio = model.generate( text="Hello, welcome to Confucius4-TTS.", lang="en", prompt_wav="path/to/reference.wav", verbose=True, ) torchaudio.save("output.wav", audio.cpu(), model.sample_rate) ``` ## 🚀 Fine-Tuning Confucius4-TTS follows a "speech encoder + LLM" architecture. The training pipeline covers two modules: - **Text2Semantic (T2S)**: generates semantic token sequences from text and speaker conditioning. - **Semantic2Acoustic (S2A)**: a flow-matching model that converts semantic tokens into mel spectrograms. ### 1. Prepare Pretrained Models Download the two external models: ```bash # Wav2Vec2-BERT (speaker conditioning & semantic feature extraction) huggingface-cli download facebook/w2v-bert-2.0 \ --local-dir pretrained/w2v-bert-2.0 # Amphion MaskGCT (semantic codec implementation) git clone https://github.com/open-mmlab/Amphion.git external/Amphion ``` After downloading, your directory should look like: ``` checkpoints/ ├── t2s_model.safetensors # pretrained T2S weights ├── s2a_model.pt # pretrained S2A weights ├── wav2vec2bert_stats.pt # semantic feature normalization statistics ├── special_tokens_map.json # tokenizer files ├── tokenizer.json ├── tokenizer.model └── tokenizer_config.json pretrained/ ├── w2v-bert-2.0/ # Wav2Vec2-BERT model └── campplus/ └── campplus_cn_common.bin # CAMPPlus speaker encoder checkpoint external/ └── Amphion/ # MaskGCT semantic codec implementation ``` ### 2. Prepare Training Data Training data is provided as **TSV files** (tab-separated, no header) with the following 5 columns: | Column | Description | |---|---| | `lang` | Language code (e.g. `zh`, `en`, `ja`) | | `wav_path` | Path to the target audio | | `norm_text` | Normalized text | | `semantic_ids_path` | Pre-extracted semantic tokens (`.npy` file path) | | `ref_audio_paths` | Reference audio path(s), comma-separated for multiple | Configure the train/validation paths in `config/train_t2s.yaml`: ```yaml data: train_data_path: - data/train.tsv val_data_path: - data/val.tsv ``` ### 3. Launch T2S Training Set the pretrained T2S checkpoint path in `config/train_t2s.yaml`: ```yaml paths: t2s_checkpoint: checkpoints/t2s_model.safetensors ``` **Single-node training:** ```bash python -m confuciustts.cli.train_t2s -c config/train_t2s.yaml ``` ### 4. Launch S2A Training Set the checkpoint paths in `config/train_s2a.yaml`. `t2s_checkpoint` points to the frozen T2S backbone; `s2a_checkpoint` is optional and can be used to resume from a pretrained S2A model: ```yaml paths: t2s_checkpoint: checkpoints/t2s_model.safetensors s2a_checkpoint: checkpoints/s2a_model.pt # optional: resume from pretrained S2A ``` **Single-node training:** ```bash python -m confuciustts.cli.train_s2a -c config/train_s2a.yaml ``` During S2A training, the T2S model, speaker encoder (Wav2Vec2-BERT), and style encoder (CAMPPlus) are all frozen. Only the flow-matching S2A model is trained. ## 📊 Performance Confucius4-TTS achieves competitive results on multilingual and cross-lingual zero-shot TTS benchmarks, with strong intelligibility and speaker similarity across multiple languages. > Lower is better for WER/CER (↓), and higher is better for SIM (↑). ### CV3-eval Cross-lingual
